articles.title: Waverley paddle steamer marks 80th anniversary since launch
articles.summary: The Waverley passed through London's Tower Bridge as part of the anniversary voyage on the Thames.
articles.body:
The world's last sea-going paddle steamer has marked 80 years since it was first launched on Glasgow's River Kelvin.

The Waverley passed through London's Tower Bridge earlier, as part of an anniversary voyage on the Thames.

Now based on the River Clyde, the ship has been restored to its original 1940s style. It makes nostalgic trips around UK ports and is one of the most recognisable historic vessels in the world.

More than 150,000 passengers have travelled on the steamer every summer for the past three years.

Waverley: 50 years of the paddle steamer bought for £1

The enduring allure of The Waverley paddle steamer

Waverley finally sets sail after two years

The oil-fired steamship replaced an earlier PS Waverley that was lost during the evacuation of Dunkirk in 1940.

It was intended for cruises up Loch Long and Loch Goil and became a familiar sight for generations of Glaswegians going "doon the watter" for their holidays.

Entering service with the London and North Eastern Railway (LNER) Clyde paddle steamer fleet on 16 June 1947, it eventually ended up being owned by Caledonian MacBrayne.

In 1974, after being withdrawn from active service, it was gifted it to the Paddle Steamer Preservation Society for £1.

Since then it has operated on a not-for-profit basis and has carried six million passengers on routes around the UK.

Waverley was launched at the Pointhouse Yard of A&J Inglis in Glasgow on 2 October 1946 by Lady Matthews, the wife of the LNER chairman.

It was the last steamer built for the company, which also operated the Flying Scotsman steam locomotive.

She noted the "splendour of the Clyde coast scenery should be viewed from steamers like this".

Passengers on the anniversary voyage down the Thames included David Horne, LNER managing director, who was there to honour the railway's role in the vessel's history.

Paul Semple, general manager of Waverley Excursions, said it was a "remarkable achievement" for the paddle steamer to have reached 80.

"She was built to serve the Clyde coast and, 80 years later, she continues to give tens of thousands of people the opportunity to experience the joy of travelling by steam," he said.

"From her early beginnings with LNER to her survival as a working paddle steamer after being gifted for £1 to the Paddle Steamer Preservation Society, Waverley has become much more than a ship.

"She is a living piece of maritime history and a much-loved part of our national heritage."

The Waverley will continue sailing on the River Thames until 11 October, before returning to Scotland for the final weekend of her 2026 anniversary season.

It will return to Glasgow and the Clyde coast for two final sailings on 17 and 18 October, bringing her 80th anniversary season to a close on home waters.

articles.title: In the 1980s, Japan buried coal fly ash beneath the sea to create solid ground for a giant bridge; after decades, the unusual foundation still supports its towers
articles.summary: When engineers in Japan began work on the Hakucho Ohashi Bridge in Hokkaido in the 1980s, they faced an unusual problem beneath the water.
articles.body: When engineers in Japan began work on the Hakucho Ohashi Bridge in Hokkaido in the 1980s, they faced an unusual problem beneath the water. The foundations for the bridge's two main towers had to be built on a soft seabed about 14 to 17 metres underwater. Instead of filling the construction area with conventional sand or soil, engineers developed a self-hardening slurry made partly from coal fly ash, an industrial waste product. The material was placed underwater inside steel cofferdams to create artificial islands that became working platforms for the bridge's tower foundations. The unusual approach reduced pressure on the cofferdams while allowing the material to harden underwater. The bridge opened in 1998, and subsequent research found that the coal-ash material continued gaining strength for more than a decade.Japan faced a difficult foundation problem beneath the seaThe Hakucho Ohashi, also known as the Muroran Bay Bridge, was planned across the entrance to Muroran Port in Hokkaido. Its main span stretches 720 metres, while the complete bridge is 1,380 metres long. Construction of the bridge began in 1985, and the completed structure opened to traffic in June 1998. The locations selected for the bridge's main towers presented a major construction challenge. The seabed was about 14 to 17 metres below the water surface and consisted of soft ground. Engineers needed to create a working platform around each tower foundation before excavation and construction could begin. A conventional approach would have involved filling the enclosed area with large quantities of sand or other material. However, the weight of conventional fill would have generated substantial pressure against the steel cofferdam surrounding the construction area. Engineers therefore searched for a material that could be placed underwater, flow into the enclosed space and eventually harden.Coal fly ash became the unusual building materialThe solution was a slurry containing coal fly ash, volcanic ash, cement and seawater. Fly ash is the fine powder collected from the exhaust gases of coal-fired power stations. Instead of treating the fly ash as waste requiring disposal, engineers incorporated it into a self-hardening construction material. The slurry could be pumped into the underwater cofferdams and allowed to harden in place. The resulting artificial islands were about 67 metres in diameter and provided working platforms for construction of the bridge's two main towers. The quantities involved were substantial. Between October 1988 and January 1989, engineers placed approximately 53,600 cubic metres of slurry into one of the cofferdammed areas. The mixture contained about 46.1 gigagrams of fly ash, 22.2 gigagrams of volcanic ash and 2.6 gigagrams of cement. The unusual material effectively turned industrial waste into solid construction ground beneath the sea. Once the slurry had hardened sufficiently, workers could excavate through the artificial island and construct the tower foundation.The mixture reduced pressure on the temporary structureThe engineering properties of the slurry were central to the project. A 1992 paper published in the Journal of Materials in Civil Engineering found that the self-hardening material generated substantially lower lateral earth pressure against the cofferdam than conventional sandy fill. That reduced the forces acting on the temporary steel structure and helped limit bending and displacement. The material also generated heat as it hardened. Researchers reported that the temperature inside the slurry remained above 10°C during construction, even under winter conditions, helping the material develop strength. This allowed the artificial island to serve as a stable working platform while engineers excavated the required area and constructed the massive concrete foundation of the bridge tower. The approach also provided a large-scale use for fly ash and volcanic ash, converting materials that would otherwise have required disposal into part of the construction process.The coal-ash material kept gaining strengthThe unusual material continued to attract scientific attention after the bridge foundations had been completed. Researchers carried out long-term investigations into the hardened slurry to determine how its properties changed with age. One of the most striking findings was that its unconfined compressive strength continued increasing for more than 10 years after placement. The continued strengthening was linked to hydration reactions within the material. Researchers also found that the long-term strength development depended on the characteristics of the coal ash used in the mixture. The findings demonstrated that the hardened slurry did not simply reach its final strength shortly after construction. Its internal reactions continued for years, gradually increasing its strength. By the time the bridge construction was completed in the late 1990s, the artificial islands had already served their primary purpose: giving workers a solid platform from which to build the main tower foundations over the soft seabed.The bridge has stood for more than two decadesThe Hakucho Ohashi Bridge opened to traffic in 1998. It is 1,380 metres long and has a 720-metre central span, making it one of the major suspension bridges in eastern Japan. The bridge has continued to serve road traffic around Muroran for more than 25 years. Maintenance work over the decades has included repairs to sections of its pavement and deck protection. The coal-fly-ash foundation method remains one of the unusual engineering features of its construction. What began as a solution to a difficult underwater foundation problem transformed industrial waste into an engineered material capable of creating solid ground beneath the sea. Coal fly ash, volcanic ash, cement and seawater were mixed into a self-hardening slurry, placed inside underwater cofferdams and turned into artificial islands. Those islands provided the working ground needed to construct the bridge's massive tower foundations. Decades after the material was placed beneath the waters of Muroran Bay, the bridge continues to stand above it, making the project an unusual example of industrial waste being transformed into the ground on which major infrastructure was built.You use AI every day. articles.title: Warring out, Pargat Singh in: Has Congress solved Punjab crisis or created more confusion?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The churn in Punjab Congress is now complete. Or is it?
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The churn in Punjab Congress is now complete. Or is it?Amarinder Singh Raja Warring is out and Pargat Singh is the new Punjab Congress president. The change came hours after Warring resigned from the post, ending his more than four-year stint as state party chief. Warring met Rahul Gandhi on Friday and formally submitted his resignation. A day earlier, he had changed his X bio to “Former PPCC President”, signalling the leadership change."He (Rahul Gandhi) gave me a lot of love. He sought information about the current political situation in Punjab, on what is happening with the government and what we should be doing there," Warring said after his meeting.Hours later, the Congress announced the appointment of Pargat Singh as the new Punjab Congress president with immediate effect. The party also appreciated the contribution of outgoing president Warring.The change in Punjab Congress comes after months of infighting over who should lead the Congress into the 2027 assembly election. The crisis was triggered by Congress’s decision to retain Warring as state unit president in July, ignoring the claims of former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi. So, Warring’s exit marks a victory for Channi and his supporters, but the entry of Pargat Singh means he does not gain from Warring's loss.Warring is out, but not downWarring may be out of his post, but has dropped strong hints that his fight may be far from over. Hours after formally stepping down, Warring targeted his detractors, signalling he is not leaving the field yet. If Warring’s remarks against party incharge Sachin Pilot are an indication to go by, we could well see a reversal of roles in Punjab Congress infighting.In an interaction with news agency ANI, Warring said. “I feel that Sachin Pilot must have decided it was time to remove ‘Raja’ from the post.” Warring, though, added that he had “no concrete proof” of this.Warring added he had not spoken to Pilot about his exit, but had heard that the state Congress incharge may have recommended a change. “Perhaps the in-charge mentioned that Raja Warring would have to be replaced,” he said when asked about the reasons for his resignation.Taking digs at those responsible for his exit, Warring said nobody had formally asked him to resign. Instead, he had simply read the “direction of the wind”."Just like elder women who could tell by reading the direction of the wind whether it was going to rain... I observed the situation closely, and it never reached the point where someone had to ask me to resign," Warring told IANS.That, he said, was why he changed his X bio to “Former PPCC President” even before formally submitting his resignation to Rahul Gandhi.The timing and the turn of events are hard to miss. Nearly a month ago, Congress removed former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel as Punjab in-charge after the Channi faction openly rebelled against him. Baghel was accused of favouring Warring and was eventually replaced by Sachin Pilot.But now, Warring appears ready to open a front against Pilot and, of course, also Channi.That also raises questions about whether replacing Baghel with Pilot has actually helped Congress settle the Punjab crisis. Sugata Srinivasaraju, senior political analyst and author, believes that the leadership change appears to have created more confusion rather than resolving the crisis at hand."What is it that the Congress saw in Pilot that they did not see in Baghel? If you thought Baghel was part of the problem, now Pilot has also become part of the problem. He’s not part of the solution," he said.According to him, Congress may now have ended up with an even bigger problem. "All of them were against Warring. Now Warring goes out and Channi has not been catered to. So we don't know what's going to happen."Both Baghel and Warring are now out of their roles in Punjab Congress. For the Channi camp, it means one of their biggest demands has been met. But with Pargat Singh in the chair, will today's change end weeks of internal feud and bickering in Punjab Congress? Perhaps not.To understand why Warring’s exit and Pargat's entry may not be the end of the crisis, it helps to go back to where the tussle began.How the Channi-Warring tussle beganThe crisis began on July 1, when the Congress leadership announced that Warring would continue as Punjab Congress president and Channi would head the campaign committee. Senior leaders Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa and Vijay Inder Singla were also given specific roles for the 2027 assembly election.On paper, it looked like an attempt to balance competing camps. In practice, it did the opposite.Channi’s supporters questioned why Warring was being retained as state chief and began pushing for a larger role for the former chief minister. What was meant to settle the leadership question instead reopened old faultlines within the party.Warring had been appointed Punjab Congress president after the party’s crushing defeat to AAP in the 2022 assembly election. Channi had been the party’s chief ministerial face in that campaign but lost both seats he contested.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Warring was then brought in by the Congress high command (read Rahul Gandhi) to rebuild the organisation and prepare it for the next election. For nearly four years, however, the Congress did not clearly announce who would lead its 2027 campaign.When it finally tried to do that in July, the compromise pleased no one.Bhupesh Baghel, who was then Punjab in-charge, tried to defuse the tussle between the Channi and Warring camps but was also caught in the crossfire and forced out of the state.His replacement, Sachin Pilot, initially managed to bring the rival factions onto the same stage during the Congress protest over the Gulzar Singh suicide case. But that show of unity did not last long.What followed was another round of meetings, complaints and feedback to the high command and, eventually, Warring's exit and Pargat's entry.Warring out, but Channi not inThe Congress high command acted swiftly after Warring's exit and handed over the baton to Pargat Singh. The three-time Congress MLA from Jalandhar Cantt and former Indian hockey captain who has served as Punjab cabinet minister in Charanjit Singh Channi cabinet, has his task cut out.Pargat's name was doing the rounds along with other key contenders which included, former MLA Rana KP Singh, Raja Sansi MLA Sukhbinder Singh Sarkaria, former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi and Gurdaspur MP Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa. But the frontrunner before today's appointment was former PWD minister and MP Vijay Inder Singla, who was appointed chairperson of the Congress Election Management and Coordination Committee in the July reshuffle."I am a loyal soldier of the party, and at all times, as a worker of the party, whatever responsibility I have been given, I have always fulfilled my duties. And in the coming times as well, we will work together with everyone in the same manner," Singla had said earlier reacting to speculations that he could replace Warring.However that did not happen.And this is where the leadership change in Punjab Congress becomes more interesting.The Channi camp had openly demanded that the former CM should lead the party into the next elections. In fact, their contention all along was that Warring should be replaced by Channi. But today's announcement would leave them disappointed much like the other contenders including Singla.2022 rerun in PunjabWith the Congress picking up Pargat Singh as the compromise candidate, it is a rerun of what happened in the run up to the 2022 elections.And that brings Punjab Congress back to a very familiar problem of bitter power tussle between state leaders. A problem that played a key role in the party’s defeat in 2022.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Ahead of the 2022 assembly election, then chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh and Navjot Singh Sidhu were locked in a bitter leadership battle. Sidhu wanted a bigger role in leading the party into the election, while Amarinder resisted attempts to cut into his authority.The Congress leadership allowed the dispute to drag on until the crisis became impossible to contain. Eventually, Amarinder Singh was removed as chief minister. Charanjit Singh Channi emerged as the compromise candidate of Congress high command and was made the chief minister.But the compromise did not end the factional war. Congress went into the election divided and suffered a historic defeat, with AAP sweeping into power.Four years later, the names have changed, but the problem looks strikingly similar.Srinivasaraju sees a larger pattern in Punjab Congress's repeated leadership tussles."Punjab Congress has not been able to resolve it at all. They've had five long years after Amarinder Singh’s exit and they have still not got it right," he said.His argument is that every time Congress begins to see a chance of returning to power in Punjab, competing factions become more active and start weakening the organisation from within."We have seen that with Navjot Singh Sidhu and Amarinder Singh," he said, adding that similar mistakes "seem to be getting repeated".Once again, both the rival leaders - Channi and Warring - are out. But the battle for Channi is still half won. And with Warring all set for a rebel role, the road ahead for the former Punjab chief minister may not be easy.With Warring’s loss not translating into Channi's gain, it will be interesting to see if the Congress's compromise candidate ends this leadership fight once and for all without starting another power tussle?Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: The G7 nations on Friday announced that they agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil from reserves over four months, including a “substantial” release of diesel in the first 20 days, as fuel prices surge amid the war with Iran, while Trump had earlier threatened diesel exporyt ban.The International Energy Agency will coordinate the G7-led release, with member countries and partners expected to begin making oil available immediately. Macron later chaired the videoconference of G7 leaders.The announcement came as the Trump administration has been pushing European countries to make more diesel supplies available while also considering measures to keep more fuel within the US. articles.title: London Fire Brigade named in Met's investigation file on Grenfell
articles.summary: The brigade is among 20 organisations the police have compiled evidence against since 2017.
articles.body:
London Fire Brigade (LFB) and a tenants' association have confirmed they are among those facing possible criminal action over the Grenfell Tower fire.

Prosecutors were handed an evidence file on 20 organisations and firms and 54 individuals from the Metropolitan Police earlier this week.

LFB and Kensington and Chelsea Tenant Management Organisation (KCTMO) have been criticised for failings relating to the fire and will find out next year if they will be prosecuted.

The Met is seeking charges including corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences and fraud offences over the deaths of 72 people in the 2017 disaster.

The Met's investigation - Operation Northleigh - began soon after the fire in June 2017 and has involved hundreds of investigating officers.

The CPS said any charging decisions would be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster in 2027.

In a statement, the LFB said: "The London fire commissioner has been notified by the Metropolitan Police Service that, following its investigation into the events surrounding the Grenfell Tower fire, a file has been submitted to the CPS for its consideration in respect of London Fire Brigade.

"The London fire commissioner welcomes the progress in the investigation process and reaffirms his commitment to providing the CPS with full cooperation, as LFB has sought to do throughout Operation Northleigh."

The commissioner, Jonathan Smith KFSM, said: "We remember the 72 people who lost their lives, and our thoughts remain with the bereaved, survivors and everyone whose lives were changed forever by that night.

"We continue working with our partners across government and the fire and rescue sector to ensure the lessons of the Grenfell tragedy are learnt, and this continues to shape everything we do."

KCTMO, facing corporate manslaughter charges, said: "We remain acutely conscious of the terrible impact of the Grenfell Tower fire on the bereaved, survivors, their relatives and the wider Grenfell community, and continue to offer our deepest condolences and sympathies to all those affected."

Most of the organisations facing potential prosecution have not been named.

Among those that have been revealed so far are the local authority Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC), which could be prosecuted for three offences: corporate manslaughter, section 3 of Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, and acting contrary to the Regulatory Reform (fire safety) Order 2005.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, which is responsible for building safety, is also among those referred to the CPS.

The fire started in the kitchen of a fourth floor flat and then spread rapidly on the outside of the building via combustible cladding.

A public inquiry found the fire was avoidable and set out how a chain of failures across government and the private sector led to the disaster.

In a report following the first phase of the inquiry, chair Sir Martin Moore-Bick condemned LFB's "serious shortcomings" and systemic failures in its response to the fire.

He concluded that fewer people would have died in the blaze if the LFB had taken certain actions earlier.

LFB said it had accepted the findings of the inquiry and had implemented all the recommendations from both phases.

Grenfell United, a bereaved families and survivors group, has previously criticised the time frame for prosecutions.

Earlier this week, the group said: "It has taken more than nine years to get here. Nine years, and no-one has been held criminally accountable for the deaths of our 72 loved ones.

"We want those responsible to face justice."

articles.title: Grangemouth firm took £1m of public money months before closure announcement
articles.summary: Syngenta says it will pay back the Scottish Enterprise funding in full if operations cease at its Grangemouth site.
articles.body:
A chemical firm collected £1m of Scottish Enterprise funding to create new jobs - just months before announcing plans to close its Grangemouth site.

The cash was part of £2.2m awarded to Syngenta in May last year to expand production at the plant.

Union leaders are meeting with the UK and Scottish governments after nearly 400 jobs have been put at risk.

Syngenta said it would pay back the Scottish Enterprise funding in full if operations cease at the site.

The company said it had been unable to make its business at the plant "competitive" in the face of "increasing international competition".

A total of 377 workers are set to be affected by the move.

A Syngenta spokesperson said: "Scottish Enterprise's grant was awarded in support of a capital investment of close to £15m that Syngenta itself has made at the site as part of efforts to diversify activity and try and secure the site's future.

"To date we have received around half of the grant allocation (about £1m), which we intend to repay in full to Scottish Enterprise if we cease operations at Grangemouth post consultation."

Hundreds of jobs under threat at Grangemouth chemical plant

New £150m funding package to protect jobs at Grangemouth

It is the latest job loss blow to the area following the closure of the nearby oil refinery in April last year, which also resulted in the loss of about 400 jobs.

In March, bus manufacturer Alexander Dennis announced plans to close its Falkirk plant with 115 roles lost, and focus its Scottish operations on the nearby Larbert site.

The UK government, under then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, previously pledged an additional £200m in funding for Grangemouth from the National Wealth Fund.

Local MP Brian Leishman had a meeting with the company earlier, which he said went "poorly".

Syngenta says a final decision has yet to be taken and it will "continue to consider options".

But Leishman questioned whether the company was having a "genuine consultation" on the future of the site.

He said: "Syngenta have offered one final solution and that is the closure of the plant.

"The whole purpose of a consultation is to try and figure out how we can get a path of saving jobs. That seems to be off the table here.

"They have announced that they plan to close the site by the end of 2027 - that seems very final to me. The workers deserve an awful lot better."

The Labour MP said the closure was a "Scotland-wide issue", adding: "We saw, with the closure of the refinery, over £400m disappear out of Scotland's economy.

"There's going to be a huge implication for Scotland's economy with Syngenta closing."

He urged the prime minister to "do the right thing" and save the site, similar to how the UK government saved British Steel .

"We're talking about 377 jobs on site - we will be talking about thousands of jobs in the wider supply chain," said Leishman.

"A huge piece of Scotland's manufacturing base. Scotland deserves better."

Reindustrialisation Minister Blair McDougall said the UK government would continue to work closely with Syngenta to explore all options for the site and the workforce.

He said: "I know this will be a deeply concerning time for workers at Syngenta and their families, and I met with the company yesterday to discuss all options for the site and the workforce.

"We worked closely with Syngenta and the Scottish government to explore every possible avenue to support them, but the company has now made this commercial decision.

"We remain committed to supporting jobs in Grangemouth following the hundreds we have already protected, and will work urgently with the National Wealth Fund in the next few days to explore all options for the area."

Leishman urged both the Scottish and UK governments to work together and not turn the issue into a "political football".

Syngenta said it had undertaken a "detailed review" of its Grangemouth operation prior to the plans being announced.

It said the Grangemouth site was "significantly more expensive" to operate than other production facilities.

The company added that savings had been identified in some areas of the business, but these fell short in "bridging the site's competitiveness gap".

Mike Hollands, president of Syngenta UK, said: "The workforce at Grangemouth is highly skilled and passionate, but despite all efforts, we have not been able to make the Grangemouth site competitive compared to alternative supply options."

articles.summary: Israeli investigators are expected to question the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking the captain and attempting to crash a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, as
articles.body: Israeli investigators are expected to question the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking the captain and attempting to crash a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, as part of a UAE-led investigation into the incident, according to a source briefed on the probe.The co-pilot was transferred from Saudi Arabia to the United Arab Emirates on Thursday after being detained in the kingdom following the emergency landing of flydubai flight FZ1073 at Tabuk.The source cited by Reuters claimed that Israeli officials were expected to question him in the UAE, although it was not immediately clear which Israeli agency would take part.An Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would participate in the UAE-led investigation alongside Emirati authorities to establish what happened and examine the suspect's motives and background.The UAE foreign ministry did not immediately comment on whether Israeli officials would directly question the co-pilot.UAE probe examines motive and possible planningThe UAE state news agency reported on Thursday that Emirati authorities had opened an investigation to establish the circumstances and motives behind the incident and determine “whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction”.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was also investigating whether the co-pilot had acted under the direction of another party. In a video statement released by his office, Netanyahu said whoever was involved would pay a “heavy price”.Netanyahu had said on Thursday that the co-pilot, whom he identified as an Omani national, had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination” and was suicidal. However, the motive for the attack has not yet been established.The co-pilot's identity has not been publicly disclosed beyond his nationality. Omani authorities have not commented on the incident.Flight plunged more than 16,000 feetThe incident occurred on Wednesday aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 people on board, mostly Israelis.The co-pilot allegedly stabbed Indian captain Smit Machchhar inside the cockpit during the flight. Passengers and crew then subdued the attacker after Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door.A reserve flydubai pilot crew travelling on the aircraft landed the plane at Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities. Machchhar was also transferred to the UAE and is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital.According to data from flight tracker Flightradar24, the aircraft plunged about 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia.Machchhar has been hailed as a hero by Netanyahu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi for his actions during the incident.In a video call with PM Modi, Machchhar described how he struggled to recover after being attacked.“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machchhar said from his hospital bed.“I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”Israeli, UAE authorities investigate attackMost of the passengers on the flight were Israeli nationals. The incident led to the suspension of commercial flights between the UAE and Israel, with Israel preparing repatriation flights for passengers stranded in the UAE.The Ben Gurion International Airport in Tel Aviv listed Arkia and Israir flights from Dubai for late Friday and early Saturday, while El Al was expected to operate a flight from Dubai to Israel on Sunday, AP reported.The incident has also raised questions over the circumstances in which the Omani national came to be assigned to a flight to Tel Aviv.Israel does not have official diplomatic relations with Oman, and Netanyahu has said pilots from countries without such relations were not permitted to operate flights to Israel.Israeli investigators are participating in the UAE-led probe, according to the Israeli government official cited by Reuters.The investigation is expected to examine the suspect's background, the circumstances of the attack and whether he acted alone or under direction.You use AI every day. articles.title: An 1852 California Gold $50 coin from the Gold Rush era sold for $367,875 on September 6; the rare piece was one of eight territorial coins in a collection that drew 475 bids from collectors
articles.summary: An 1852 California Gold $50 piece has brought nearly $368,000 at auction, highlighting the enduring appeal of coins linked to the early Gold Rush era.
articles.body: An 1852 California Gold $50 piece has brought nearly $368,000 at auction, highlighting the enduring appeal of coins linked to the early Gold Rush era. According to the auction house GreatCollections, the rare Augustus Humbert $50 was part of its Centennial Collection of Territorial Rarities, which featured eight certified territorial coins and drew 475 bids during the collection’s auction run. The collection was presented from September 6 through September 27, 2026. The coin itself, however, was listed among the collection’s September 6 offerings and sold for $367,875, including the buyer’s fee. Its rarity, preservation and connection to early California gold make it one of the standout pieces from the collection.A coin from California’s Gold Rush eraGreatCollections identified the 1852 piece as an 1852 California Gold $50 U.S. Gold Assay Office Augustus Humbert 887 Reeded Edge, graded PCGS MS-63+. It was produced during the period when California’s enormous gold discoveries created an urgent need for reliable forms of gold-based currency. The coin was associated with the U.S. Assay Office in San Francisco and Augustus Humbert, an official United States assayer who produced large gold pieces during the early years of the California Gold Rush. GreatCollections describes territorial gold as privately or locally issued gold produced when federal coinage was scarce, including issues connected to the California, Georgia, Colorado and Utah gold rushes.These pieces are commonly known as “slugs,” reflecting their unusual size and appearance compared with conventional United States coins. Their historical importance comes partly from the monetary conditions of the period, when gold discovered in California needed to be assayed, weighed and converted into forms that could be used in commerce.Rare Augustus Humbert $50The 1852 $50 piece carries the Augustus Humbert name and the designation “887,” referring to its fineness. According to GreatCollections, the coin was struck at .887 fine to reflect the natural purity of California placer gold. It also described the piece as the rarest of three Humbert Reeded Edge varieties. Its condition was another factor that distinguished the coin. Rather than showing the extensive wear often associated with early territorial gold, the example was graded MS-63+, indicating that it retained a high level of preservation.GreatCollections also described it as the finest known example of the variety by two full grade points. The auction house said the coin had exceptional preservation and strong remaining detail for a historic Gold Rush issue. GreatCollections identified it as a plate coin in America’s Golden Age by Donald H. Kagin and David McCarthy, highlighting its significance in numismatic literature.$367,875 auction resultGreatCollections reported that the $50 coin sold for $367,875, including the buyer’s fee. Its listing attracted 93 bids, according to the auction house’s results. The result placed the coin among the most valuable pieces in the Centennial Collection of Territorial Rarities. Another major highlight, an 1852 California Gold $10 Wass, Molitor & Company Close Date coin, sold for $354,375, including the buyer’s fee. That coin attracted 74 bids. The collection brought together eight PCGS-certified coins, with one also approved by CAC. Across the collection, GreatCollections recorded 475 bids, while hundreds of users followed the offerings during the auction period.Eight territorial raritiesThe Centennial Collection included several other early California gold pieces alongside the $50 Humbert issue. Among them were an 1852 California Gold $10 Wass, Molitor & Company coin, an 1852 California Gold $10 Moffat & Company piece, an 1854 California Gold $20 Kellogg & Company Double Eagle and an 1853 California Gold $20 U.S. Gold Assay Office coin. The collection also included two California State of California silver die trials from 1851, along with another 1852 U.S. Gold Assay Office Augustus Humbert $10.GreatCollections presented the collection between September 6 and September 27. While the collection concluded on September 27, the auction record for the $50 Humbert coin shows that its individual sale took place on September 6. The sale illustrates how pieces connected to California's earliest gold-producing years continue to attract collectors, particularly when rarity, historical provenance and exceptional preservation come together in a single coin.You use AI every day. articles.title: When the crew became the crisis: Air India’s 2009 mid-air brawl
articles.summary: The flight carrying 106 passengers from Sharjah to Delhi via Lucknow witnessed a mid-air confrontation that raised questions about cockpit discipline and
articles.body: The flight carrying 106 passengers from Sharjah to Delhi via Lucknow witnessed a mid-air confrontation that raised questions about cockpit discipline and flight safetyThe recent flydubai incident has highlighted an unusual aviation danger: what happens when those responsible for flying an aircraft become part of the crisis themselves.Captain Smit Machchhar was reportedly attacked by his co-pilot during a flight, triggering a dangerous descent before the injured captain managed to open the cockpit door and allow others to intervene. The aircraft eventually landed safely.Seventeen years earlier, an Indian Airlines (then a subsidiary of Air India) flight witnessed a mid-air confrontation that raised similar questions about cockpit discipline and flight safety.A fight at 30,000 feetOn October 3, 2009, Indian Airlines flight IC-884 was carrying 106 passengers from Sharjah to Delhi via Lucknow. While cruising at around 30,000 feet over Pakistan, Captain Ranbir Arora and co-pilot Aditya Chopra became embroiled in a dispute with flight purser Amit Khanna and flight attendant Komal Singh.Reports said the confrontation spilled between the cockpit and galley while the Airbus A320 was airborne.The dispute had begun before take-off from Sharjah.From argument to violenceIn Sharjah, the cabin crew met Captain Ranbir Arora and co-pilot Aditya Chopra for a pre-flight briefing, during which the two sides were believed to have had an altercation.“The cabin crew lobby said that after the initial tension on the ground in Sharjah, when the woman crew member [Komal Singh] went into the cockpit, one of the pilots held her hand and then pushed her out of the cockpit,” according to a TOI report. She reportedly hit the cockpit door and began bleeding.Khanna then intervened, according to a cabin crew representative, who alleged that the pilots became abusive and fought with him.The pilots denied the allegation. They instead accused Khanna of misconduct that they claimed had compromised flight safety. The pilots also alleged that the molestation complaint was “aimed to protect the complainant’s purser friend — who has a commercial pilot licence (CPL) — from facing action”, the report added.After landing in Delhi, Singh filed a molestation complaint against the two pilots.There were also reports that the cockpit was briefly left effectively “unmanned” while the confrontation continued outside. Some accounts said Arora threatened to divert the aircraft to Karachi. These claims were not independently established.Investigations and falloutSingh’s allegations triggered a separate investigation. Air India set up a five-member committee, while the National Commission for Women formed a five-member panel.Delhi Police recorded Singh’s statement and registered a molestation case.Air India confirmed the fight and ordered an inquiry, while the Directorate General of Civil Aviation initiated a probe. All four crew members were grounded.The airline’s preliminary inquiry concluded that Arora and Khanna had played a greater role. Both were suspended, while Chopra and Singh remained grounded. The Indian Commercial Pilots Association questioned the action against Arora, saying the findings were not final.Air India later filed departmental chargesheets against all four. Singh was charged with participating in the altercation, failing to leave the cockpit when directed and speaking to the media in breach of company policy.Arora faced allegations including abusive language and pushing Khanna and Singh from the cockpit, while Khanna was accused of initiating the fight.An airline official said the preliminary inquiry found all four guilty of some charges, including conduct that tarnished the company's reputation.The episode became more than a workplace dispute. It showed how a personal conflict among crew members can spill into an aircraft's operational environment — and put flight safety under strain.Read the detailed storyThe 2009 Air India Brawl at 30,000 feet that put 106 passengers at riskGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Suzy Lamplugh Trust urges women's safety standards across hotels
articles.summary: Travelodge is working with Suzy Lamplugh Trust to elevate safety standards for women and girls.
articles.body:
A charity working with a hotel chain to tackle violence against women and girls following an independent review is calling for industry-wide standards.

Travelodge is consulting with personal safety charity Suzy Lamplugh Trust (SLT) after a review of the chain found guests were still not as safe as they should be.

The review came after the BBC revealed how a woman woke up to a man sexually assaulting her in her bed at the chain's Maidenhead branch in December 2022 after staff gave him a key card and her room number.

Saskia Garner, head of policy and campaigns at SLT, said the incidents highlighted in the review "need to be a wake-up call to all organisations across the hospitality sector".

Barrister Paul Greaney KC, who carried out the independent review, said the chain's security policies at the time of the attack at its Maidenhead hotel were "not fit for the purpose of keeping guests safe".

He found room intrusions reported at nearly one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, and no policy in place on violence against women and girls.

Interim chief executive of Travelodge, Ray Reidy, said the company, which is based in Thame, Oxfordshire, is working with the SLT to develop one.

Saskia Garner said the work with Travelodge is "just developing" and that the charity is working with the company "to ensure that their policies and procedures reflect and address the issues of violence against women and girls", which the charity believes "need to be urgently addressed".

She said the charity hopes this will be rolled out to all staff "imminently".

Garner said the incidents that have been highlighted in the review "should never have happened".

"It absolutely needs to be a wake-up call to all organisations across the hospitality sector to ensure that nothing like this ever happens again and that their policies and procedures and training are fit for purpose and that their staff understand how these behaviours play out and ensure that every preventative measure is put in place to ensure no one ever experiences anything like this again."

In the review, Greaney said room intrusions were a problem across the hotel sector.

Garner said: "Given the prevalence of violence against women and girls in society, I think it's almost certain that these issues [highlighted in the review] will not be confined to one particular hotel chain.

"That is why we are calling for industry-wide standards and training to ensure the highest level of implementation, knowledge and understanding about violence against women and girls and how that manifests in the hotel context."

The review of Travelodge makes 38 recommendations, including moving towards a system that requires guests to show ID to get a room key, which Travelodge has been trialling at some hotels since May.

Reidy said: "Nobody is working harder on security of rooms in this industry than we are today.

"We embrace all of the findings in the review, we accept the recommendations and we will address all of those."

articles.title: A Mississippi homeowner spent more than a decade building a waterfront house styled after the Taj Mahal; the unfinished 4,402-sq-ft home, listed for $2 million in 2016, is back for $2.5 million
articles.summary: An unfinished waterfront mansion inspired by the Taj Mahal is back on the market in Ocean Springs, Mississippi, with a new asking price of $2.5 million.
articles.body: An unfinished waterfront mansion inspired by the Taj Mahal is back on the market in Ocean Springs, Mississippi, with a new asking price of $2.5 million. The 4,402-square-foot property sits on nearly an acre along the Gulf Coast. It was first listed for $2 million in 2016. Ten years after that first listing, and 13 years after construction began, the steel-and-concrete home is still unfinished. It is waiting for a buyer willing to complete its ambitious design. Building permits for the property were first filed in 2008 by Biloxi doctor Dr Pravin Saija, according to the Sun Herald. Saija planned to use the home as his main residence. But finding contractors who could follow the project's detailed plans proved difficult, slowing the work over the years. Rachel Allen, a listing agent with Coastal Realty Group, told Realtor.com that the owner has chosen to sell the property instead of finishing the remaining work himself. "The owner started building the home 13 years ago and had trouble finding a contractor to finish the vision the way he wanted," Allen told Realtor.com. "Since then, it has been left as it was, and it fell to the wayside. The seller is ready to retire, move on, and let someone else finish the vision."Intricate layout and structural foundationsThe five-bedroom home stands 30 feet above sea level and has 126 feet of direct water frontage. It was built with insulated concrete forms. The main structure, foundation, and outside walls are all in place. The design includes south-facing turrets with water views and large outdoor terraces for seating. There is also a primary bedroom suite on the top floor and a distinctive tower that could be turned into guest quarters. The property has a rooftop lounge area as well, although the roof now needs structural repairs. The main structural work is finished, but the inside is still an empty shell. Finishing the home will require basic utility systems, including complete electrical wiring and plumbing. Drywall, interior fixtures, kitchen countertops, and cabinets will also need to be installed. Allen estimated to Realtor.com that finishing the inside and cleaning up the grounds would cost between $800,000 and $1.2 million. The final cost would depend on the materials and finishes chosen by the new owner. "The construction of it is magnificent, and it is 30 feet above sea level," Allen explained to Realtor.com. "The most expensive parts have already been done. We wanted to show what the house could be. A lot of people appreciate seeing the potential."Material costs drive updated valuationThe $500,000 increase from the 2016 asking price reflects changes in local property values and the current value of construction materials already on the property, according to the listing agent. "It could be completely done in about six months," Allen told Realtor.com. "The reason for the increase in price is the increased cost of additional materials that are also available." Marketing materials for the property include computer-generated pictures of possible finished interiors. They are shown alongside photographs of the unfinished concrete structure to help potential buyers picture what the home could look like when completed. "What makes this listing so compelling is not simply its size or architecture," Allen said. "It is the mystery, history, and enormous potential behind it. People want to see inside it, understand why it was never completed, and imagine what it could ultimately become." Allen said the current owner thought about finishing the work before putting the property up for sale. In the end, he decided not to take on the project. "He hopes someone makes it how they want it," she said.Flexible usage options on the coastThe property is about 20 minutes from downtown Ocean Springs and has no restrictions on short-term rentals. According to Coastal Realty Group, the estate could be used as a private home, a corporate retreat, a wedding venue, or a boutique hotel. Any commercial use or redevelopment would still have to follow local zoning rules and receive the required building permits and administrative approvals. Ocean Springs has also received wider attention as a coastal destination. It recently appeared on a USA Today list of the top beach communities to live in. Because the property has a specialized design and would require a large investment to finish, real estate agents expect much of the interest to come from outside the local area. "Most likely, it will not be someone already living in the local market," Allen told Realtor.com. "This property will require a buyer with a unique vision, the resources to complete it, and the ability to recognize an opportunity unlike anything else currently available on the Gulf Coast."You use AI every day. articles.title: AI and the monk: Anthropic goes for swami and friends to tame Claude
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: When Silicon Valley runs into a problem it cannot solve with computing power, it usually hires more engineers and
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: When Silicon Valley runs into a problem it cannot solve with computing power, it usually hires more engineers and programmers, usually from India. Anthropic went one better: it convened a gathering of religious scholars, philosophers, and theologians, including a monk from India, to discuss an increasingly vexing question: What, exactly, is this thing we are building and what should be its guardrails?Among those invited to its San Francisco headquarters early this year was Swami Sarvapriyananda, a scholar of Advaita Vedanta who heads the Vedanta Society of New York. He has since publicly confirmed that Anthropic flew him to California for a philosophical salon connected with training Claude and with AI ethics. “Details I cannot give because they have something called an NDA, a non-disclosure agreement,” he said in a public talk in June that surfaced online recently.Still, he said, Anthropic showed the participants some of its latest work, including Mythos and Project Glasswing.One of Anthropic’s founders, Christopher Olah, who leads work on understanding the internal workings of AI systems and was present throughout the engagements, discussed with participants the possibility that models can display behaviour resembling human emotions and personality.Sarvapriyananda is an unusually apt person for Anthropic to have put around the table because his speciality is Advaita Vedanta -- the non-dual philosophical tradition associated with the Upanishads and Shankara -- and increasingly, the intriguing territory where consciousness meets neuroscience, physics and AI.A monk of the Ramakrishna Order, he joined the organisation in 1994 after an MBA from the Xavier Institute in Bhubaneswar and took sannyasa, or final monastic vows, in 2004.After years of teaching and working in Ramakrishna Mission institutions in India and serving in Southern California, he became a spiritual leader of the Vedanta Society of New York in 2017. He was also a Nagral Fellow at Harvard Divinity School in 2019–20.His lectures on the Mandukya Upanishad, the tiny Upanishad devoted to the nature of consciousness and the significance of Om, have become popular online, accumulating millions of views.Anthropic itself has acknowledged the program, revealing it had spent months talking with scholars, clergy, and ethicists from more than 15 religious and cross-cultural traditions, including Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism, Sikhism and Islam.The company says it wants Claude to absorb from all these traditions rather than adopt one; to learn from faiths that have spent centuries thinking about virtue, character, moral responsibility and what constitutes a good life. Such conversations could influence Claude's constitution, the values reinforced during training, and behaviours used in safety evaluations.Sarvapriyananda says Anthropic's researchers appeared simultaneously excited and alarmed by the trajectory of AI. According to a report in the NYT, they have been asking religious and philosophical thinkers to take seriously the possibility that advanced AI might possess some form of consciousness or moral status.One participant, Rabbi Abraham Navon, a former computer engineer whose doctoral work examined machine consciousness, came away with the impression that Anthropic researchers were discussing Claude less like a piece of software and more like a potentially conscious entity deserving moral consideration.While Sarvapriyananda has argued in his discourses that AI could potentially reproduce functions associated with intelligence because, in Vedanta, intellect and mind are themselves objective phenomena, pure consciousness is another matter.He has repeatedly distinguished intelligence from consciousness and questioned whether computational machinery can produce awareness rather than merely simulate the behaviour associated with an aware being.Effectively, Anthropic is attempting something unprecedented: compressing millennia of human reflection on virtue, suffering, responsibility, compassion and the good life into a training process for an entity that may be neither human nor entirely understood.In one experiment inspired by discussions about moral formation, Anthropic gave Claude a tool that could remind it of its ethical commitments before consequential actions. The company says the experiment reduced certain forms of misaligned behaviour in internal evaluations.Did Claude applaud? No word on that.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Texas is putting hundreds of tons of concrete and railroad ties into the Gulf; the material is being turned into new fish habitat
articles.summary: Off the Texas coast, hundreds of tons of cement railroad ties, concrete structures and other durable materials are being placed on the floor of the Gulf
articles.body: Off the Texas coast, hundreds of tons of cement railroad ties, concrete structures and other durable materials are being placed on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico to create new habitat for marine life. The latest example is the HI-54 Deep Artificial Reef Project, a 160-acre reef site that reached a major milestone in summer 2026 after years of planning and coordination. According to a Port Arthur LNG report published on August 25, 2026, the completed reef includes 300 pyramids, 102 cement culverts, 400 tons of cement railroad ties, 100 low-relief habitat plates, 17 quarry rocks and numerous cement piling cut-offs. Port Arthur LNG and industry partners, including Bechtel, its engineering, procurement and construction contractor, contributed materials and funding to the project. Clean, unused concrete culverts that had been staged at the Port Arthur LNG project site were also incorporated into the reef.The project is the third artificial reef developed through a partnership involving the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD), Coastal Conservation Association Texas, Friends of Sabine Reefs and industry partners. Port Arthur LNG contributed a $125,000 partnership investment, which the company said was aligned with its climate action and biodiversity priority. The funding supported the purchase and deployment of additional reef pyramids as well as the transportation and placement of materials at the site.How concrete structures become fish habitat in the GulfThe principle behind an artificial reef is relatively simple. Much of the Gulf seabed off the Texas coast is a broad, relatively featureless expanse of mud and sand, with little naturally hard substrate for marine organisms to colonise. Artificial reef structures provide stable surfaces and spaces where marine life can establish itself. TPWD says the materials used for artificial reefs must be complex, stable and durable, with openings that can provide shelter for marine animals. Concrete and heavy-gauge steel are among the principal materials used by the program, while concrete culverts, purpose-designed pyramids, bridge materials, retired petroleum platforms, ships and quarry rock can all become components of reef sites. All reefed materials must meet federal and state environmental guidelines.The department says nearly 200 marine fish species have been seen around its artificial reef structures. Scientific divers have also recorded red snapper at TPWD artificial reef sites during four out of every 10 visits. Texas currently has artificial reef sites covering 3,440 acres across state and federal waters in the Gulf, including nine sites within nine nautical miles of shore that provide relatively accessible fishing and diving opportunities. TPWD's program has been operating on a much larger scale than the HI-54 project alone. More than 140 petroleum platforms have found new purpose as marine habitat through the Texas Artificial Reef Program.Inside the HI-54 Deep Reef projectThe HI-54 Deep Reef uses a mixture of purpose-built and repurposed materials rather than relying on a single type of structure. The 300 pyramids and other reef components create physical complexity on the seafloor, while the 102 cement culverts and hundreds of tons of cement railroad ties add additional hard surfaces and shelter. The Port Arthur LNG account says clean, unused concrete culverts from the company's project site were also reused in the reef rather than remaining as surplus construction material. That approach is consistent with the broader TPWD program, which specifically identifies concrete, heavy-gauge steel, culverts, bridge materials and other durable structures as potential reef materials. The department says materials must be inspected and meet environmental requirements before they can be deployed.The project also brought together private industry and conservation groups. Port Arthur LNG identified Bechtel, its engineering, procurement and construction contractor, as one of the industry partners contributing to the effort. Jim Thompson, permitting and compliance manager for Sempra Infrastructure, described the collaboration as a way for industry and conservation groups to work toward a shared habitat goal. “This project reflects what can be accomplished when industry and conservation partners work together with a shared purpose,” Thompson said. Mic Cowart of Friends of Sabine Reefs similarly pointed to the potential benefits for both conservation and recreational fishing, saying the completed reef would support marine life and create new fishing opportunities.From artificial reefs to sunken shipsConcrete and railroad ties are only part of Texas' approach to creating artificial marine habitat. The state's program also includes entire vessels and retired offshore petroleum structures. TPWD says 13 ships have been intentionally sunk as part of its Artificial Reef Program. The largest is the USTS Texas Clipper, a 473-foot vessel now serving as a reef off South Padre Island. Before the ship was reefed, crews removed hazardous materials and other contaminants, including hydrocarbons, asbestos, PCBs and debris. The Texas Clipper also demonstrates the economic role that artificial reefs can play. TPWD says the ship reef generates more than $1 million for the local economy from anglers and between $1.4 million and $2 million from divers. The department reports average spending of $460 per fishing trip and upwards of $2,000 per dive.Artificial reef programs are not unique to Texas. TPWD says 16 of the 23 U.S. coastal states, or about 70%, maintain artificial reef programs. In Texas, the system combines purpose-built reef structures, repurposed concrete and steel, retired petroleum platforms and deliberately sunk vessels. The HI-54 Deep Reef adds another 160 acres to that network. Its hundreds of structures and 400 tons of cement railroad ties are intended to create the hard, complex surfaces that marine organisms and fish can use, turning a collection of construction and industrial materials into another piece of underwater habitat along the Texas Gulf Coast.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mexico to propose bill to restrict violent social media content after school attack
articles.summary: Mexico president Claudia Sheinbaum on Friday said her government is expected to pass a bill next week requiring social media companies to remove content
articles.body: Mexico president Claudia Sheinbaum on Friday said her government is expected to pass a bill next week requiring social media companies to remove content that encourages violence.This follows Thursday's horrific attack at a school in Mexico's northern Coahuila state, which left a deputy principal dead and four people hospitalised. The perpetrators were reportedly 18 years old and were taken into custody immediately."The goal is for digital platforms to take on some of the responsibility and refrain from disseminating, promoting, or spreading content related to this type of information — including criminal acts or violent behavior," Sheinbaum stated in her daily news conference.The government would look for a bill, regulation, or other legislative framework that would mandate compliance from all social media sites, she said.Sheinbaum said the proposal is aimed top protect young people in Mexico from exposure to violence, while adding that authorities remain willing to engage in dialogue with the platforms, as per the reuters.The European Union, Australia, and the United Kingdom are among the nations that have enacted legislation mandating social media companies to take down violent content.Brazil has taken the strongest step in Latin America, with its Supreme Court ruling in 2025 that social media platforms must remove content that encourages violence. articles.title: New visa rules in Australia from October 2: No more visa hopping for international students, agents selling 'false hope' under scrutiny
articles.summary: Australia unveiled its new visa rules effective from October 2, 2026 which will put a stop to \"permanently temporary migration\" and will also crack down
articles.body: Australia unveiled its new visa rules effective from October 2, 2026 which will put a stop to "permanently temporary migration" and will also crack down on visa agents and immigration lawyers who are selling "false hope" to foreigners about how they can continue to live in Australia. International students can't keep on studying in Australia just to stay in the country and now they will have to apply for a separate visa if they want to transfer courses. Also, one can't apply for a lower-grade course after completing a higher-grade course only to remain in Australia on a student visa. This means a student can't switch to vocational training from a bachelor's or master's degree because it is then evident that they just want a visa to stay in Australia.'When Australians go to another country'Assistant minister for international education, Julian Hill, said the changes in the visa rules are aimed at stopping the increase of "permanently temporary" migration.“When Australians go to another country, they do not believe they have some God-given right to hop around from visa to visa for years or decades and game other nations’ appeals and courts systems – and neither should guests in our country,” Hill said.Hill said that from July 1, 2027, a student’s visa will not be extended even if they are transferring into a different course, to prevent “rorting and ensures students can’t just not turn up for the first 6 months, fail their subjects then go to a cheaper provider”.In a social media post, the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said: “As of today there are new rules to put an end to student visa hopping. It’s all about ensuring we have a migration system that Australians can be confident in.” Migration agents and lawyers selling “false hope” by helping individuals to pursue baseless visa claims to help them stay in Australia longer will also be targeted under new rules.What is visa hopping?Tony Burke explained that there are individuals who would never meet the qualifications to become a permanent resident and so they would hop from one visa category to another, and then they will use the appeal process so that they can stay in Australia as long as possible until it eventually becomes absurd not to let them stay, because at that point they have Australian citizen children and they are also integrated into the local community.You use AI every day. articles.title: Norwich Theatre staff reported to police for theft
articles.summary: The theatre says the investigation also found staff had created "inappropriate" graffiti.
articles.body:
Former staff working for a theatre company have been reported to the police for theft following an investigation into misconduct.

The BBC understands the allegations relate to a number of staff formerly working at Norwich Theatre's Playhouse bar, who have now been dismissed.

A smaller number of the ex-employees have also been accused of creating "inappropriate graffiti", the theatre said.

A spokesperson added it has been "forced" to make the allegations public after the union Unite announced staff were joining as members following "serious concerns about a series of dismissals". The union said its members deny the allegations.

A Unite spokesperson said: "Our members deny there has been any theft of the theatre's property or any other wrongdoing. And our members will co-operate in full if they are asked to meet with the police."

At the time of the dismissals, Unite claimed Norwich Theatre had denied workers the right to trade union representation.

Norwich Theatre "strongly refuted" any suggestion it had acted unfairly or unlawfully.

The row prompted Clive Lewis, Labour MP for Norwich South, to publicly back Unite and its Norwich Theatre members in their pursuit of formal union recognition.

The dismissals came to light in August following a statement being issued by the union.

Norwich Theatre said at the time it could not comment due to an ongoing investigation into "extremely serious matters" but this had now concluded.

It said it had taken "decisive disciplinary action... given the seriousness of theft from a charity" and the case had been reported to the police.

A spokesperson added: "It is unfortunate that this situation found its way into the public domain.

"This was not our choice, but because of this, we are forced to make the outcome of the investigations public as well. We would have preferred to handle this privately.

"There was no need for this to play out in public and we do not believe this was in the best interests of the individuals concerned or any of Norwich Theatre's people."

Unite and Norfolk Police have been approached for comment.

Norwich Playhouse is the sister venue to the larger Theatre Royal.

It is about to undergo a major refurbishment, with work expected to start in 2028.

articles.summary: Pakistan’s federal government and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) agreed to hold a second round of talks on
articles.body: Pakistan’s federal government and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) agreed to hold a second round of talks on Saturday, as the opposition party prepares for a long march towards Islamabad from October 4.The first round of negotiations was held on Friday in the chamber of national assembly speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, who is facilitating the dialogue amid heightened security in the capital.According to a statement issued by the National Assembly Secretariat, the participants held detailed discussions “on the prevailing political situation and exchanged views on various matters of national importance”.“The government, PPP and opposition representatives apprised each other of their respective positions and held a detailed exchange of views constructively and cordially. The participants emphasised the need to resolve national issues through dialogue and negotiations,” it said, according to news agency PTI.The second round will be held at 2 pm on Saturday in the speaker’s chamber.Sadiq said he was “only playing the role of a mediator”, adding that his office was “always open” to resolving issues through negotiations.“Parliament is the only forum where solutions to issues can be found,” he said, stressing that negotiations were the way to address political differences.PTI international spokesman Zulfiqar Bukhari said the talks were “primarily aimed at defusing the current political situation surrounding PTI’s planned march/protest toward Islamabad on October 4”.Bukhari said the party’s demands included an “immediate” meeting with Khan and a decision to take him to hospital so his personal doctors could examine him. PTI has also sought the release of Khan’s sisters and others arrested ahead of the protest, a medical check-up for his wife Bushra Bibi and proper hearings in their cases.Meanwhile, the Pakistan authorities have deployed additional police and placed shipping containers on routes into Islamabad. articles.title: Elizabeth Mata bought 94 acres in North Carolina in 1973; an I-540 corridor later restricted 9.93 acres for nearly 20 years before the state Supreme Court sent her compensation case back for valuation
articles.summary: A long legal fight over land restrictions tied to a road project in North Carolina has reached a key point.
articles.body: A long legal fight over land restrictions tied to a road project in North Carolina has reached a key point. The state Supreme Court has sent a Wake County landowner's compensation case back to trial judges so they can decide how much the property was worth. Elizabeth Mata bought 94 acres of land in 1973. Decades later, state transportation officials set aside a 9.93-acre strip across her property for the planned Interstate 540 outer loop. The restriction limited her ability to build on or sell that part of the property for nearly 20 years. The North Carolina Supreme Court ruled that the restrictions imposed under the state's former Map Act amounted to an indefinite taking of property rights. The justices sent the case back to a lower court to decide exactly how much money the North Carolina Department of Transportation (NCDOT) must pay Mata.Decade-long restrictions on private propertyThe dispute began with the Transportation Corridor Official Map Act, a state law passed in 1987. The law allowed the NCDOT to file maps showing the planned routes of future highways. Once a map was filed with local officials, owners of property inside the marked area could not get building permits or develop their land. State officials said the law was meant to control infrastructure costs. By stopping development in areas planned for future roads, the state could avoid higher costs later. But the restrictions left thousands of acres across North Carolina in legal uncertainty for long periods, without the state officially buying the affected land. In Mata's case, state officials filed a corridor map in 1996 for an extension of the I-540 outer loop around Raleigh. The planned highway route covered 9.93 acres of her 94-acre property. This effectively stopped development on that part of the land. The North Carolina General Assembly repealed the Map Act in 2019 after a series of legal defeats. The repeal came after a major 2016 ruling by the North Carolina Supreme Court in Kirby v. North Carolina Department of Transportation. That ruling found that corridor map filings were an unconstitutional taking of private property rights and required the state to provide just compensation under eminent domain rules.Valuation disputes and legal argumentsAlthough lawmakers repealed the law, dozens of lawsuits were still open over how courts should calculate payments for owners affected by old corridor maps. During arguments before the North Carolina Supreme Court, attorneys for the NCDOT argued that the 2019 repeal changed the historical restrictions into temporary takings. The state's lawyers said damages should cover only the period when the corridor map was officially active. Howard Rhodes, an attorney for the NCDOT, told the justices during oral arguments reported by the Carolina Journal that property owners affected by the Map Act should be fully compensated once. Rhodes argued that treating the restrictions as indefinite would require the department to pay much more than earlier legal decisions required. He said the state was trying to provide fair compensation under Supreme Court guidance. Mata's lawyers argued that filing the corridor map created an indefinite restriction on her property rights. They said the restriction could not later be called temporary simply because lawmakers repealed the law. Her legal team said the state had effectively controlled the parcel for almost 20 years, greatly reducing its value and limiting how it could be used.High court ruling and next stepsIn its ruling, the North Carolina Supreme Court again found that corridor map filings created takings of indefinite duration, rather than short-term restrictions. In its opinion, the justices said the state's original action permanently limited basic property rights from the date the map was recorded. The Supreme Court overturned lower court decisions that had used different methods to calculate compensation. It ordered the trial court to reconsider the damages using established legal standards for indefinite takings. The ruling now allows a Wake County trial judge to hold hearings and determine the exact amount of money Mata should receive for the 9.93-acre section of her property. According to court filings in the North Carolina Judicial Branch docket system, the case will now return to Superior Court. Real estate appraisers and expert witnesses are expected to present evidence about the property's exact value and the financial effect of the state's long-running restrictions.You use AI every day.
